::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## How to use this document

Every grey block below is a prompt you can type straight into the Posit Assistant pane
in **RStudio** or **Positron**. The brown note underneath explains what makes it an
*IDE* prompt rather than a generic chatbot prompt — that distinction is the whole point
of this session.

Read the prompts out loud once, then change the file names, column names and variable
names to your own. A prompt that names *your* objects is worth ten generic ones.
:::

# Before you type a single prompt

Five minutes of setup buys you four days of better answers.

1. **Open the Assistant.** In RStudio, click the Assistant button in the toolbar
   (RStudio 2026.04.0 or later; you may be asked to *Install Posit Assistant* the first
   time). In Positron, the Assistant pane is on the right and became the default AI
   experience in Positron 2026.07.
2. **Sign in to a model provider** — Posit AI, or your own Anthropic / OpenAI / Gemini /
   Bedrock key. Settings live in `~/.posit/assistant/settings.json` globally and
   `.posit/assistant/settings.json` per project.
3. **Always work inside an RStudio Project or a Positron workspace folder.** The
   Assistant reads relative paths. Outside a project it is guessing.
4. **Type `/trust` once per workspace** so memory files and skills are allowed to load.
5. **Confirm your session is attached.** The Assistant automatically attaches your active
   editor file and your live R or Python session. That attachment is the source of its
   power: it can see your Variables pane, your data frames, your active plot, and it can
   run code in *your* console. If the attachment is missing, click the paperclip and add
   **Interpreter Sessions…**
6. **Set thinking effort.** Off or Low for boilerplate, Medium for wrangling, High for
   modelling and debugging.
7. **Start in a safe mode.** Leave permissions at **Normal** for the workshop. Use
   `/restricted` if you want to confirm every tool call, and keep `/yolo` for the day you
   trust it and are in a Git repository.

::: {.callout-important}
## The one habit that separates a good prompt from a bad one

A generic AI tool has to be *told* what your data looks like. Posit Assistant can
**look**. So never paste a `head()` output into the chat. Say *"look at the data frame
`pslm` in my session"* instead. Every prompt in this document is built on that difference.
:::

# The house rules

Before the prompt library, five rules. Teach these on Day 1 morning and refer back to them
all week.

**Rule 1 — Name the object, don't describe it.** `hies_2024` beats "my household survey
data". The Assistant can inspect the first; it can only imagine the second.

**Rule 2 — State the destination.** "Write this into `R/01-import.R`" or "add this as a
new chunk below the setup chunk". An answer that lands in the right file is worth more
than a better answer in the chat pane.

**Rule 3 — Ask for the check, not just the code.** "…then run it and show me the row
count before and after" turns a suggestion into evidence.

**Rule 4 — Constrain the dialect.** Say *tidyverse*, say *base R*, say *data.table*.
Say *no new packages*. Your workshop participants must be able to read the answer.

**Rule 5 — Plan before you build.** For anything longer than one function, open with
`/plan`. You will review the design, not debug the debris.

# Day 1 — Orientation, projects, and getting data in

## Meeting the IDE

::: {.prompt}
I am completely new to R. In two short paragraphs and no code, explain what the four
panes of this IDE do and where my code actually runs.
:::
::: {.why}
The Assistant knows which IDE you are in, so it describes the panes in front of you rather
than a generic screenshot from a blog post.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Set up this project the way an experienced R user would. Create the folders, add a
`.gitignore` suitable for R and Quarto, and create an `AGENTS.md` that records that this
project uses the tidyverse, Quarto, and British English spelling. Show me the plan first.
:::
::: {.why}
The Assistant writes real files into your real project folder. `AGENTS.md` is then loaded
automatically at the start of every future conversation in this workspace, so the
convention sticks for the rest of the week.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Check my session: list the packages that are loaded right now, my R version, and tell me
which of the tidyverse packages I still need to install.
:::
::: {.why}
This is a session query, not a knowledge question. It reads the live interpreter, so the
answer is about *this* machine in *this* room.
:::

## First import

::: {.prompt}
Look at the files in the `data-raw/` folder of this project. For each one, tell me what
format it is, roughly how big it is, and the single best function to read it into R.
Don't import anything yet.
:::
::: {.why}
It inspects the actual folder. Participants with different files each get a different,
correct answer — which is exactly the moment a room stops feeling like a lecture.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Import `data-raw/hies_2024.csv` into a tibble called `hies`. Read the first few lines
first and choose the column types explicitly rather than letting readr guess. Run it, then
show me `dplyr::glimpse(hies)` and tell me which columns were read as character but look
numeric.
:::
::: {.why}
Three moves in one: it reads the file header itself, executes in your console, and reports
back a diagnosis of your specific data. No generic AI can do the middle step.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Import every sheet of `data-raw/pbs_tables.xlsx` into a named list of tibbles, keeping the
sheet names. Show me the dimensions of each sheet in a small summary table.
:::
::: {.why}
Multi-sheet Excel is where beginners lose an hour. The Assistant can open the workbook and
count the sheets before writing the loop.
:::

::: {.prompt}
The file `data-raw/labour_force.dta` is Stata format. Import it, keep the variable labels
as an attribute, and print a table of variable name, label, and class so I can see what I
actually have.
:::
::: {.why}
Labelled survey data is the daily reality for economics and statistics participants, and
the Assistant can read the label attributes out of the live object.
:::

::: {.prompt}
This CSV has three junk rows above the real header and a totals row at the bottom. Read
the file, show me the first 12 raw lines so we agree on what is junk, then write an import
that skips them and drops the totals row.
:::
::: {.why}
"Show me the raw lines so we agree" is the move to teach. It forces the Assistant to
evidence its assumption before writing code on top of it.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Connect to the DuckDB file `data/pbs.duckdb`, list the tables and their row counts, and
show me the first 10 rows of the largest one without pulling the whole table into memory.
:::
::: {.why}
The Assistant sees your Connections pane and can query through the live connection, so it
writes `dplyr` against the database rather than guessing at a schema.
:::

## When it goes wrong

::: {.prompt}
(Click "Fix" beside the error in the Console.)
:::
::: {.why}
The Console error actions — **Fix** and **Explain** — are one click, no typing. Fix
diagnoses the error and proposes a corrected line; Explain walks through what the code was
trying to do. Show this early; it removes the fear of red text.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Explain this error message to someone who has never programmed. Then tell me the two most
common causes, and check which of them applies in my session.
:::
::: {.why}
The second sentence is the one that matters — it checks *your* environment instead of
listing possibilities.
:::

---

# Day 2 — Cleaning and wrangling

## Diagnosis before treatment

::: {.prompt}
Profile the data frame `hies` in my session. For every column report: type, number of
missing values, number of distinct values, and for numeric columns the min, median and
max. Flag anything that looks suspicious and tell me why. Do not fix anything yet.
:::
::: {.why}
The single most useful prompt in this whole document. It reads the object in memory,
so the report is about your data, and "do not fix anything yet" keeps the participant in
charge.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Look at the character columns in `hies` and tell me which ones are really categorical.
For each, show me the distinct values sorted by frequency, and point out any that look
like the same category spelled differently.
:::
::: {.why}
Spotting `"Punjab"`, `"punjab"` and `"PUNJAB "` requires seeing the values. The Assistant
can tabulate them in your session and bring back the evidence.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Check `hies` for duplicate records. First on the id column alone, then on the full row.
Report the counts, show me three example duplicates, and only then suggest what to do.
:::
::: {.why}
"Report, show examples, then suggest" is a reusable prompt shape. Write it on the
whiteboard.
:::

## Fixing

::: {.prompt}
Clean the column names of `hies` to lower snake_case, but show me a before-and-after
mapping table first so I can veto any rename I dislike.
:::
::: {.why}
The veto step. Automated renaming silently breaks downstream scripts; a mapping table
turns a black box into a decision.
:::

::: {.prompt}
The column `income` in `hies` is character because it contains commas, currency symbols
and the string "N/A". Convert it to numeric. Before and after, print how many values are
NA so I can confirm nothing was silently lost.
:::
::: {.why}
The before/after NA count is the reproducibility habit in miniature — and the Assistant
runs it, so the numbers are real.
:::

::: {.prompt}
The `date_of_interview` column has mixed formats: some dd/mm/yyyy, some yyyy-mm-dd, some
Excel serial numbers. Show me examples of each pattern from my data, then write a single
robust parser and report how many rows still fail.
:::
::: {.why}
It samples the actual mess rather than assuming a format, which is the difference between
code that runs and code that runs *on this file*.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Reshape `hies` from wide to long: the columns from `exp_food` through `exp_transport`
should become `category` and `amount`. Use tidyr, run it, and show me the dimensions
before and after so I can see the shape change.
:::
::: {.why}
Pivoting is abstract until the participant watches 4,000 × 12 become 48,000 × 3 in their
own Variables pane.
:::

::: {.prompt}
I need to join `hies` to `districts` on district name, but I suspect the names don't
match. Before joining, show me which names in each table have no partner in the other.
Then propose a lookup table to fix them.
:::
::: {.why}
The anti-join check before the join. This one prompt prevents the most common silent data
loss in applied work, and the Assistant can execute it immediately.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Rewrite the code I have selected in the editor using modern tidyverse: `.by` instead of
`group_by()` where it fits, `join_by()` in joins, and the native pipe. Keep the output
identical and prove it by comparing the result to the original with `waldo::compare()`.
:::
::: {.why}
Selected-code context plus a proof of equivalence. Modernisation without the fear that
something quietly changed.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Turn the cleaning steps we just did into a function called `clean_hies()` in a new file
`R/clean.R`, with roxygen documentation and defensive checks on the input columns. Then
source it and confirm it reproduces the object currently in my session.
:::
::: {.why}
The end-of-day move: exploration becomes a file, and the file is verified against the
session it came from.
:::

---

# Day 3 — Analysis, graphics and models

## Exploring

::: {.prompt}
Using the data frame in my session, compute mean and median household expenditure by
province and by urban/rural, with the number of observations in each cell. Present it as
a tidy table, then tell me in plain language what stands out.
:::
::: {.why}
Code plus interpretation, grounded in the numbers it just computed rather than in
plausible-sounding generalities.
:::

::: {.prompt}
This survey has a weight column `wt`. Redo the provincial means using the weights, put the
weighted and unweighted figures side by side, and tell me where they differ most and what
that implies about the sample.
:::
::: {.why}
Survey weighting is the substantive point for a statistics audience, and the comparison
table makes the lesson visible instead of theoretical.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Suggest three plots that would reveal something genuinely interesting in this data. For
each, say in one line what question it answers. Then draw the first one.
:::
::: {.why}
It has seen the columns and types, so the suggestions are about your variables — a much
better teaching moment than "consider a scatter plot".
:::

## Graphics

::: {.prompt}
Improve the plot currently showing in my Plots pane: proper axis labels with units, a
title that states the finding rather than the variables, a colourblind-safe palette, and
`theme_minimal()`. Explain each change in one line.
:::
::: {.why}
The Assistant can see the **active plot**. "Improve the plot in my Plots pane" is a
sentence that only makes sense inside this IDE, and it always lands well in a room.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Turn this ggplot into a small-multiples version faceted by province, keep the y-axis free,
and order the facets by median value rather than alphabetically.
:::
::: {.why}
Reordering facets by a statistic requires knowing the statistic; it computes it from your
data first.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Save this figure as `figures/expenditure-by-province.png` at 8 × 5 inches and 300 dpi, and
also write the ggplot code into `R/fig-expenditure.R` so I can regenerate it.
:::
::: {.why}
Two artefacts, both on disk, both reproducible. The figure alone is not a deliverable.
:::

## Modelling

::: {.prompt}
Fit a regression of log expenditure on education, age, household size and province using
the data in my session. Before you fit, tell me which variables have missing values and
how many rows the model will actually use. Then fit it and produce a tidy coefficient
table.
:::
::: {.why}
The row-count warning before fitting. Listwise deletion silently shrinking a sample is the
classic quiet error, and the Assistant can count it in advance.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Run the standard diagnostics on the model object `m1` in my session, show me the plots,
and tell me in plain language whether any assumption looks violated and what I might do
about it.
:::
::: {.why}
`m1` is a live object. The Assistant inspects it directly rather than asking you to paste
`summary()` output.
:::

::: {.prompt}
/predictive-modeling-r

Set up a tidymodels workflow to predict poverty status from the variables in my session:
a recipe with sensible preprocessing, a logistic regression and a random forest, 5-fold
cross-validation, and a comparison of ROC AUC. Explain each step as you go — my audience
is new to machine learning.
:::
::: {.why}
`/predictive-modeling-r` invokes the built-in tidymodels skill explicitly, so you get
Posit's own house patterns rather than whatever the model half-remembers from Stack
Overflow.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Compare the two model objects in my session and produce a single table of coefficients,
standard errors, R-squared and number of observations, formatted for a report.
:::
::: {.why}
It reads both objects from the environment. Nothing is retyped, so nothing is mistyped.
:::

---

# Day 4 — Quarto, reproducibility and parameterised reporting

This is the day the Assistant stops being a coding helper and becomes a reporting
assistant. Slow down here.

## Building the document

::: {.prompt}
/quarto-authoring

Create a Quarto HTML report at `reports/expenditure-report.qmd` with a floating table of
contents, code folding on, figure captions, and a setup chunk that loads the tidyverse and
reads the cleaned data. Leave placeholder sections for Introduction, Data, Findings and
Conclusion. Do not fill them in yet.
:::
::: {.why}
The `quarto-authoring` skill carries Posit's own Quarto conventions. Invoking it by name
is more reliable than hoping it triggers on its own.
:::

::: {.prompt}
/report

Turn everything we have done in this conversation into a Quarto document: the cleaning
decisions, the tables, the plots and my reasoning. Keep my commentary, drop the dead ends.
:::
::: {.why}
`/report` is the command participants remember for the rest of their careers. An afternoon
of exploration becomes a documented `.qmd` in one line — the analysis writes its own
narrative.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Read my `.qmd` and give every code chunk a meaningful label, plus `#| fig-cap:` for
figures and `#| tbl-cap:` for tables. Then add cross-references in the prose so the text
says "see @fig-expenditure" instead of "see the figure below".
:::
::: {.why}
It edits the real file in place. Cross-referencing is tedious by hand and instant here.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Render this document and, if it fails, read the error, fix it, and render again. Tell me
what was wrong. Don't ask me to copy the error message — you can see it.
:::
::: {.why}
The render–fail–fix loop, executed by the Assistant in your terminal. This is the single
most convincing demo of agentic behaviour for a Quarto audience.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Rewrite the Findings section of my `.qmd` in plain language for a policy audience,
keeping every number exactly as computed. Do not invent a figure that is not in the
results.
:::
::: {.why}
The instruction to preserve computed values is the guardrail. State it every time you ask
for prose about numbers.
:::

## Making it reproducible

::: {.prompt}
Audit this project for reproducibility. Check for absolute file paths, `setwd()`,
`rm(list = ls())`, hard-coded numbers in the prose that should be inline code, and any
data file that is read but not present in the repository. Give me a prioritised list of
fixes.
:::
::: {.why}
It walks your actual project tree. Every participant leaves with a to-do list for their
own work, which is far more persuasive than a slide of best practices.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Find every place in my `.qmd` where I typed a number that was computed in the analysis,
and replace it with inline R code so it updates when the data changes. Show me each
replacement for approval.
:::
::: {.why}
This is the definition of a reproducible report, done as a mechanical edit on the real
document.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Set up `renv` for this project, snapshot the current library, and add a short section to
the README explaining how a colleague would restore the environment.
:::
::: {.why}
It runs the commands and writes the documentation in one pass, so the environment and its
instructions never drift apart.
:::

::: {.prompt}
#changes

Look at what I have changed on this branch and write a commit message: a short subject
line and a body explaining why, not what.
:::
::: {.why}
`#changes` pulls your recent branch changes into the prompt. There is also a sparkles icon
in the Source Control commit box that does this in one click.
:::

## Parameterised reporting

This is the crown of Day 4. Build it in four prompts, in this order.

::: {.prompt}
/plan

I want to turn `reports/expenditure-report.qmd` into a parameterised report that can be
rendered separately for each province. Plan the change: what parameters, what has to move
into the setup chunk, what happens to the title, and how the outputs get named. Ask me
anything that is ambiguous before you write code.
:::
::: {.why}
`/plan` puts the Assistant into design mode. It explores the file, asks questions, and
proposes an approach before touching anything — and the participants see that the *design*
conversation is where the value is.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Now implement the plan. Add a `params` block with `province` defaulting to "Punjab", make
the title dynamic so it reads "Household Expenditure — Punjab", and replace every
hard-coded province filter with `params$province`. Then render it once with the default to
prove it still works.
:::
::: {.why}
Implement, then prove. Never accept a parameterisation you have not seen render.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Write `render-all.R` that loops over the four provinces, renders the report for each with
`quarto::quarto_render()`, and writes the output to `reports/output/expenditure-<province>.html`.
Run it and list the files that were produced.
:::
::: {.why}
The moment one report becomes four is the emotional peak of the workshop. Have the
Assistant run it live and list the files.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Extend `render-all.R` so it also produces a PDF and a Word version of each report, and
writes a small `index.qmd` linking to all of them. Handle the case where a province has
too few observations by writing a short note instead of failing.
:::
::: {.why}
Graceful failure is the difference between a demo and a pipeline. Ask for it explicitly.
:::

::: {.prompt}
/savememory

Record in this project's memory that reports are parameterised by province, rendered
through `render-all.R`, and that outputs go to `reports/output/`. Future conversations in
this project should follow that pattern.
:::
::: {.why}
`/savememory` writes to `AGENTS.md`. Tomorrow morning's conversation starts already
knowing how this project works — which is what makes the Assistant feel like a colleague
rather than a stranger.
:::

---

# The one-hour revision session

Do not lecture. Put these on screen one at a time and let participants type them into
their own projects. Ten minutes each, six prompts, done.

::: {.prompt}
Look at my project and tell me, in five bullet points, what this analysis does. Write it
for someone who has never seen it.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Profile the main data frame in my session and tell me the three things I should have
checked but didn't.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Find the weakest piece of code in this project — the part most likely to break when the
data is updated next quarter — and explain why, without fixing it yet.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Render every Quarto file in this project. Report which ones succeed, which fail, and why.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Quiz me. Ask five questions about the R code in this project, one at a time, wait for my
answer, and tell me whether I am right. Start easy and get harder.
:::
::: {.why}
Turning the Assistant into an examiner is the highest-value five minutes of any revision
hour, and it draws its questions from the participant's own code.
:::

::: {.prompt}
/context

Show me what you currently know about my session and how much of it you are using.
:::
::: {.why}
Ending on `/context` demystifies the whole thing. Participants see exactly what was sent
and stop imagining either magic or surveillance.
:::

---

# Presentation day

::: {.prompt}
/quarto-authoring

Turn `reports/expenditure-report.qmd` into a revealjs presentation of about 12 slides.
Keep the figures, cut the code, and rewrite the prose as spoken bullet points. Use a dark
green (#2C5F2D) and muted brown (#8B7355) theme with Georgia for body text.
:::
::: {.why}
The report already exists and is already correct. The deck is a rendering of it, not a
retyping — which is the reproducibility argument made visible.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Read my slides and write speaker notes for each one: what to say, roughly how long, and
the single number I must not forget to mention.
:::

::: {.prompt}
Act as a sceptical discussant. Read my analysis and give me the five hardest questions
someone in the audience could ask, with a one-line answer for each.
:::
::: {.why}
It has read the actual code and results, so the objections are real methodological ones,
not generic seminar questions.
:::

---

# A little Python, in the same window

Positron and RStudio both run Python. The Assistant sees whichever session is active — so
switch the console, and the same prompt shape works.

::: {.prompt}
Switch my active session to Python. Read the same CSV with pandas, and show me the polars
version side by side. Then tell me which one you would teach a beginner and why.
:::

::: {.prompt}
I have a data frame in my R session and I want to continue in Python. Show me how to move
it across with reticulate, and confirm the row count matches on both sides.
:::
::: {.why}
Cross-language work is the reason many people move to Positron. The confirmation step is
what makes it trustworthy.
:::

::: {.prompt}
/predictive-modeling-python

Build a scikit-learn pipeline for the same prediction problem we solved with tidymodels
this morning, and compare the results honestly.
:::

---

# Anti-patterns

Show these deliberately. A wrong prompt beside a right one teaches faster than either
alone.

| Don't type this | Type this instead |
|---|---|
| "Here is my data: [pastes 40 rows]" | "Profile the data frame `hies` in my session." |
| "Write code to clean data" | "Column `income` in `hies` is character; convert it to numeric and report the NA count before and after." |
| "Fix my code" | "Read `R/clean.R`, run it, and tell me why line 34 fails." |
| "Make a nice plot" | "Improve the plot in my Plots pane: axis units, a finding-based title, colourblind-safe palette." |
| "Build me a whole dashboard" | "/plan — I want a Shiny dashboard with three tabs. Propose a structure first." |
| "Is this analysis correct?" | "List the assumptions this analysis makes that I have not tested, then test the two most important." |
| "Redo everything" | "/compact, then: starting from the cleaned data, ..." |

::: {.callout-warning}
## Two rules that are not negotiable

**Never let generated code go into a report unrun.** If the Assistant wrote it, execute it
and look at the output. Posit is explicit that it does not support or assist with
AI-generated code — the correctness is yours.

**Never send data you are not permitted to send.** Session context includes variable names,
types and sampled values. For confidential microdata, use `positron.assistant.aiExcludes`
to exclude files, turn off implicit session context in settings, or work on a synthetic
extract during the training.
:::

# Appendix A — An `AGENTS.md` to hand out

Put this at the root of the workshop project on Day 1. It loads automatically at the start
of every conversation in a trusted workspace.

```markdown
# Project conventions

## Style
- R only unless I ask for Python. Tidyverse dialect, native pipe `|>`.
- No new package dependencies without telling me first.
- British English spelling in prose. Numbers in tables to 1 decimal place.

## Structure
- `data-raw/` is read-only. Never write to it.
- Cleaning code lives in `R/`, reports in `reports/`, figures in `figures/`.
- Cleaned data is written to `data/` as `.rds`.

## Reporting
- All reports are Quarto. Numbers in prose are inline R code, never typed.
- Reports are parameterised by province and rendered through `render-all.R`.

## How to behave
- Show me a plan before changes that touch more than one file.
- After writing code, run it and show me the output.
- If my data contradicts your assumption, tell me instead of coding around it.
```

# Appendix B — A custom skill for house style

Custom skills go in `.posit/assistant/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` for a single project, or
`~/.posit/assistant/skills/` for all your projects. Project skills override user skills,
which override the built-ins.

```markdown
---
name: pbs-tables
description: House style for statistical tables in PBS reports. Use whenever
  producing a table for a report or presentation.
---

# PBS table style

- Use `gt` for HTML, `flextable` for Word.
- Title states the finding; subtitle states the source and year.
- Thousands separators on all counts. One decimal place on percentages.
- Every table ends with a source note: "Source: Pakistan Bureau of Statistics, <survey>, <year>."
- Never abbreviate province names.
```

Then, in any conversation: `/pbs-tables — turn the summary in my session into a report
table.`

# Appendix C — Slash command cheatsheet

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `/plan` | Design first: explores, asks questions, proposes an approach before editing |
| `/ask` | Read-only mode — questions and exploration, no file changes |
| `/report` | Turns the conversation into a Quarto document |
| `/notebook` | Exports the conversation as a Jupyter notebook |
| `/savememory` | Writes project facts into memory so future sessions inherit them |
| `/context` | Shows what the Assistant currently knows and the token usage |
| `/compact` | Summarises a long conversation to free up room |
| `/microcompact` | Replaces tool results with placeholders — lighter than `/compact` |
| `/new`, `/clear` | Start fresh, keeping model and settings |
| `/trust` | Marks the workspace trusted so memory and skills load |
| `/restricted` | Confirm every tool call — good for teaching |
| `/yolo` | Run tools without confirmation — only in a Git repository |
| `/sandbox` | OS-level isolation for shell commands |
| `/mcp`, `/plugin` | MCP servers and the plugin marketplace |
| `/quarto-authoring`, `/predictive-modeling-r`, `/predictive-modeling-python`, `/shiny-bslib`, `/r-package-development` | Invoke a built-in skill directly |

Other context shortcuts worth knowing: **`#changes`** pulls recent branch changes into the
prompt, the **paperclip** attaches files, folders, commits and interpreter sessions, and
the **eye icon** on an attachment toggles whether it is actually sent.

# Appendix D — The verification ritual

Teach this as a closing habit. After any substantial piece of AI-written code, ask:

::: {.prompt}
Before I accept this: what assumptions did you make about my data that you did not verify?
Check each one against my session and tell me which hold.
:::

If the Assistant cannot verify an assumption, that assumption is your homework. That is the
honest relationship to build with these tools, and it is the note to end the workshop on.

Posit Assistant replaced the earlier Positron Assistant and Databot.*
:::
